summary: Read and verify the nine agent-learning papers Rohin referenced (MemSkill, OPD-Evolver, Meta-TTL, Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience, OEL, SEAL, TMEM, Early Experience, SDFT) and extract what each says to teach

result.title: MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents
result.authors: Haozhen Zhang, Quanyu Long, Jianzhu Bao, Tao Feng, Weizhi Zhang, Haodong Yue, Wenya Wang (Nanyang Technological University; UIUC; UIC; Tsinghua)
result.venue_or_status: arXiv preprint, ICML-formatted (keywords "Machine Learning, ICML"; likely ICML 2026 submission, acceptance not stated in the paper). Code: github.com/ViktorAxelsen/MemSkill (Apache-2.0, ~570 stars); controller weights on HuggingFace (XaiverZ/memskill). HuggingFace "#3 paper of the day" Feb 2026.
result.sections_read: Abstract; 1 Introduction; 2 Related Work; 3 Method (3.1 overview, 3.2 skill bank, 3.3 controller/executor/optimization, 3.4 designer, 3.5 closed loop); 4 Experiments (4.1 setup, 4.2 comparison, 4.3 distribution shift, 4.4 ablation, 4.5 discussion incl. cost analysis; Tables 1-3); 5 Conclusion; Appendix A (A.1-A.4: ALFWorld w/ and w/o demos, AppWorld, Llama-3.1-8B, training stability); Appendix B (B.1 eval details, B.2 designer details, B.3 ALFWorld training, B.4 PPO/Top-K objective); Appendix C (C.1 initial primitive skills, C.2 evolved LoCoMo skills, C.3 evolved ALFWorld skills, full text via PDF); Appendix D (executor, designer analysis, designer refinement, judge prompts); E, F. Also the GitHub README.
result.what_is_learned_and_how: Three things change, none of them LLM weights. (1) A small MLP "controller" (f_ctx, f_skill, f_score over a frozen Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B) is trained with PPO to select an ordered Top-K subset of "memory skills" for each 512-token span of an interaction trace, conditioned on the span and the memories already retrieved from that trace's memory bank; the reward is the downstream task score (F1 on LoCoMo QA, success rate on ALFWorld) obtained by answering memory-dependent training queries from the constructed memory bank, delivered only at the end of the trace (r_T = R, gamma-discounted). (2) A shared natural-language "skill bank", initialised with four primitives (Insert, Update, Delete, Skip), is evolved by a frozen LLM "designer" that every 100 controller steps mines a sliding hard-case buffer (difficulty d(q) = (1 - reward) x failure count, KMeans-clustered by query semantics), performs a two-stage analysis (diagnose storage / retrieval / memory-quality failures, group into patterns) then proposes at most 3 refinements or new skills per round, with best-snapshot rollback and a decaying logit bonus so the controller explores new skills. (3) A trace-specific external text "memory bank" is written by a frozen LLM "executor" (LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct at train time) that, given the span, retrieved memories and the selected skills, emits INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE action blocks in one pass. Controller and skill bank are learned at train time and frozen at deployment ("MemSkill learns and evolves the skill bank before deployment, this preparation cost is amortized"); at test time only the memory bank is built, span by span, with K=7 (conversational) or K=5 (ALFWorld) skills, and the same skill bank is transferred without retraining to Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, Llama-3.1-8B, LongMemEval, HotpotQA and AppWorld.
result.what_it_tells_us_to_parent: The paper's central move is to separate memory content from the skill of remembering: the README states the evolved skills "are NOT experiential/procedural memory/insights themselves. Rather, they are a form of meta-memory that focuses on what kinds of memory to extract, how to remember and where to focus, and what to preserve or forget." Each skill is a teachable, first-person-applicable routine in a fixed form (Skill / Purpose / When to use / How to apply / Constraints / Action type), and the initial primitives already spell out concrete write behaviours a parent could teach verbatim: "Compare against retrieved memories to avoid duplicates. Split distinct facts into separate items. Keep each item concise and specific. Skip trivial, fleeting, or speculative content" (Insert); "Merge new details into a single updated item. Preserve accurate details that still hold" (Update); "Only delete when evidence is explicit. If uncertain, prefer no action over deletion" (Delete). What the data-driven evolution then adds is a set of perception directions that the base primitives missed: on dialogue, "Capture Temporal Context" (start/end/duration/sequence), "Capture Activity Details" (type, location, participants, time), "Capture Entity Nuances" (nicknames, aliases, comparisons), "Handle Entity Relationships", "Refine Temporal Details with Context"; on embodied tasks, "Capture Action Constraints" (action-constraint pairs), "Track Object Location" (object-location-state triplets), "Track Object Movements" -- i.e. the learned lesson is "perceive events along these axes and write each as a separate item", and every evolved skill carries the constraint "Avoid inferring details not directly stated", an explicit provenance rule. The designer prompt externalises the reflective process a parent would run on the child's failures: check whether the retrieved memories contain the answer; classify as "storage failure (skill missing or misapplied)", "retrieval failure (embedding mismatch)" or "memory quality failure (memory exists but is too vague or incomplete)"; group failures "into patterns tied to information types, entities, temporal details, or constraints"; propose one concrete change to the write rules per pattern, and do not change the rules for one-off retrieval misses. The controller's job is the discretionary part -- which of these lenses to apply to this span given what is already stored -- and the ablation shows that learned selection (vs random) and evolved skills (vs the four fixed primitives) each matter, with the evolved skill bank mattering most (LoCoMo L-J 53.82 vs 46.50 with only the fixed primitives).
competencies_implied: decide what to store per span given what is already remembered
deduplicate against existing memory before writing
split distinct facts into atomic items
write concise, specific items with temporal and entity detail
capture events along fixed perception axes (time, place, participants, aliases, relations, constraints, object state)
revise/merge rather than duplicate when new detail arrives
delete only on explicit contradiction; prefer no action under uncertainty
skip trivial, fleeting or speculative content
record only what is stated (no inference) -- provenance constraint
diagnose a recall failure as storage vs retrieval vs quality
extract a reusable rule from clustered hard cases
rewrite own memory-writing instructions between training phases
compose several skills in one pass at span granularity
transfer memory skills across tasks and base models
result.relevance_to_links: Link A (the write): MemSkill is entirely about the write and confirms it is the bottleneck -- with the same frozen executor and retriever, changing only the rules that govern what gets written moves LoCoMo L-J from 46.50 (four fixed primitives) to 53.82, and random skill selection costs 5-11 points. It also shows that a write policy can be improved from a task-recall signal and that the resulting policy transfers to unseen datasets (LongMemEval, HotpotQA, AppWorld) and unseen base models (Qwen 80B, Llama 8B). But the write target is an external text store retrieved by embedding similarity, the writer is a frozen LLM following prompt text, and the memory never enters weights; nothing here tests whether the same write discipline produces good post-training data. Link B (parenting installs the form): the designer is a close analogue of our parent -- it reads the child's failures, diagnoses why the memory was missing or vague, and rewrites the child's perception routines in a fixed form (Purpose / When to use / How to apply / Constraints) -- and its evolved skills are a ready-made list of perception axes to teach ("capture temporal context", "track object-location-state", "avoid inferring what is not stated"). The difference is where the form lives: in MemSkill it is installed as prompt text that a separate MLP selects and the executor must re-read at every span forever; the child (executor) never internalises anything, which is exactly the gap our LoRA is meant to close (H1: the form expressed outside the context that taught it). The README's own distinction -- skills are "meta-memory... the way or skill of remembering, rather than the remembered content" -- is our thesis stated in their vocabulary. Link C (integrated loop improves later learning): the closed loop (use skills -> mine hard cases -> evolve skills -> resume) is shown to improve the skill bank progressively during training and to generalise, which supports the claim that a better remembering skill yields better performance on unseen tasks. It does not test H2: evolution stops before deployment, the test-time skill bank and controller are frozen, and the reward comes from ground-truth QA labels rather than from the agent's own experience, so no slope of learning-from-self-generated-experience is measured, and there is no 2x2 with consolidation on/off. Differences from our frozen base + one LoRA rewritten at sleep from the child's own thinking: (1) the learned parameters are an external MLP over frozen embeddings, not any part of the LLM; (2) memory is a retrieved text store, not weight memory via canonical-frame completion; (3) skill selection is a separate module, not the child's own thought stream, and the executor is told to emit "no explanations or REASONING lines" -- articulation is suppressed rather than trained; (4) supervision is external labels, not the child's articulated experience; (5) the write is one-pass INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE per span with dedup, whereas our regime wants repeated, varied perception of the same fact; (6) the "avoid inferring details not directly stated" constraint parallels our provenance gate, but is a prompt rule, not a mechanical check. Caveat on evidence: LoCoMo has only 10 conversations split 6/2/2, so the main conversational test set is two dialogues; the ALFWorld and AppWorld results (SR 57.71 vs 45.99 best baseline without demos on LLaMA) and cross-model transfer are the broader evidence.
result.evidence_scale: Trained with LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct as executor (API), MLP controller on A6000s; transferred without retraining to Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Headline (LLaMA): LoCoMo L-J 53.82 vs MemoryOS 48.64 / A-MEM 49.71 / LightMem 51.95 with 215 LLM calls vs 1288 (MemoryOS); LongMemEval L-J 60.89 (transfer) vs CoN 56.44; ALFWorld avg SR 80.36 vs 77.80 with in-context demos and 57.71 vs 45.99 (LightMem) without demos; AppWorld avg PR 26.71 vs 25.42 (AWM). Controls: random skill selection (w/o Ctrl, 48.43), fixed four primitives (w/o Des, 46.50), refine-only (47.45); cross-dataset and cross-model transfer; a no-demonstration ALFWorld setting to decouple ICL demos from constructed memory; span-size sweep for quality/cost. Caveats: LoCoMo has 10 conversations split 6/2/2 (two test dialogues), adversarial and abstention questions removed; LongMemEval test is ~100 stratified samples.

result.title: OPD-Evolver: Cultivating Holistic Agent Evolver via On-Policy Distillation
result.authors: Guibin Zhang*, Xun Xu*, Yanwei Yue, Zikun Su, Wangchunshu Zhou, Xiaobin Hu, Shuicheng Yan (LV-NUS Lab, FDU, PKU, ByteDance; *equal contribution)
result.venue_or_status: arXiv preprint; GitHub repo (bingreeky/opd-evolver) labels it "[EMNLP'26 Findings]". Code (partial: executor OPD path only) and a LoRA adapter for Qwen3.5-9B released at huggingface.co/greeky/OPDEvolver.
result.sections_read: Abstract; 1 Introduction; 2 Related Work; 3.1 Problem Formulation; 3.2 Fast Evolution Loop; 3.3 Slow Evolution Loop (attribution eqs. 11-12, distillation eqs. 13-16, Algorithm 1); 4.1 Setup; 4.2 Main Results (Tables 1-2); 4.3 Ablation (Table 3); 4.4 Framework Analysis (Figs 2-4); 4.5 Case Study; 5 Conclusion; Appendix A (related), C (benchmarks, C.1 protocol), D (training data and parameters), E, F (case studies); GitHub README.
result.what_is_learned_and_how: Two things change. (1) At test time, an external four-tier memory store M_t = {trajectories, tips, skills, tools} grows without weight change ("fast loop"): the same policy pi_theta selects a compact subset S_t from 50 embedding-retrieved candidates, acts conditioned on the formatted selection, then writes Delta_t (it chooses which tiers and how many items, possibly none), and every Q=30 tasks runs a multi-turn maintenance episode with lookup/merge/delete tool calls. (2) At train time ("slow loop"), the policy weights themselves change (released as a LoRA adapter on Qwen3.5-9B; Qwen3-4B-Instruct also used) via on-policy self-distillation: the student samples its own output under the deployment condition z^k, and a privileged teacher, which is the *same* model with stop-gradient, conditioned additionally on a hindsight view h^k, scores the same student prefixes; the loss is full-vocabulary token-level KL from teacher to student, summed over the four decision types k in {sel, act, write, maint}. The only external signal is the task return R_t; it is turned into dense "outcome-calibrated memory attribution" V(m): for each memory, mean return on tasks where it was selected minus mean return on tasks where it was retrieved but not selected (candidate-controlled), weighted by a selection-rate factor, a confidence factor gamma(m)=1-1/sqrt(1+N+) and a tier prior. The hindsight views are: selection sees V(m) of every candidate; execution sees the valuable selected memories plus a successful same-group trajectory while the student must solve with no memory ("internalization"); writing sees which of its own written memories later became valuable; maintenance sees value/confidence/usage/redundancy diagnostics. Training uses 7,000 tasks from AWM, Nemotron-Terminal-Corpus and EnvScaler, disjoint from all evaluation benchmarks; evaluation starts from an empty memory and accumulates only from the test stream.
result.what_it_tells_us_to_parent: The paper's core claim is precisely the one our thesis makes: "retaining experience is not the same as learning how to evolve through it", and an "agent evolver" is one that "systematically transforms interaction history and feedback into persistent improvements in future behavior." It decomposes this into four coupled, teachable behaviours with the paper's own names: (1) experience selection (from a noisy, high-recall candidate set, keep only what is causally useful for the present task; the trained selector rejects "superficially related but not causally useful" memories); (2) experience-grounded execution (act with the selected experience, and eventually without it: the "internalization" target asks the student to solve with no memory while the teacher sees the good memory and a success trajectory); (3) experience writing (from a trajectory plus its outcome, write "compact causal tips" that "target the root cause of the failure" rather than "generic advice", e.g. "Exploring adjacent is insufficient" instead of "verify the goal and add an action validator"; decide per tier how many items to write, possibly zero; the writer keeps only its top 30% by value); (4) experience management (periodically lookup/merge/delete, scoring, consolidating and retiring memories). The signal a parent could hand the child is the hindsight attribution: which memories, when present, made later episodes succeed (V(m)), i.e. teach the child to judge a written memory by its future utility, not its plausibility, and to write fewer, sharper, environment-specific, verifiable items (column names to check, the fact that reward comes only from stepping onto the goal tile, grading-specific output formats). The paper measures these dispositions directly: median calibrated score of selected memories rose 0.66-0.69 to 0.76-0.79 and of written memories 0.80-0.82 to 0.89-0.91 after distillation, and the memory-free policy gained 3-7 success points with up to 2.5 fewer steps, i.e. the write behaviour and the internalised content are both measurable independently of task score.
competencies_implied: select causally useful experience from noisy retrieval
act on selected experience, then act without it (internalize)
write compact root-cause lessons from failure, not generic advice
decide what and how much to store (discretionary writing, may write nothing)
judge a memory by its downstream utility (hindsight attribution)
periodically consolidate, merge and retire memories
convert a scalar outcome into dense supervision for read/write/maintain decisions
self-teach via privileged-hindsight view of own rollouts
result.relevance_to_links: Link A (the write): OPD-Evolver treats writing as a learned behaviour of the same policy, supervised by outcome-calibrated hindsight; its ablation shows removing writing distillation costs 5 points on CTF and its writer-quality distributions are the closest published analogue to our synthetic-vs-child-authored gap and to Rohin's discretionary-memory ruling (the count n_t^l "is chosen by the agent", tips vs skills vs tools vs trajectories mirrors graded importance). It also supplies a provenance-compatible gate: every written memory is traceable to (x_t, tau_t, R_t) and is scored only on later tasks where it was retrieved. Link B (parenting installs the form): there is no external parent; the "teacher" is the child itself given privileged hindsight, so the form of good writing is installed by self-distillation against outcome evidence rather than by a stronger model's demonstrations. This is evidence that the disposition is trainable into weights from outcomes alone, but it says nothing about whether a parent's corrections do it faster or better; our H1/H2 remain the untested comparison. Link C (integrated loop improves later learning): the paper's main and ablation results are levels on held-out benchmarks after training, with memory accumulated only during the test stream; "w/o Slow Evolution" (frozen weights, memory only) drops 33.1 vs 38.7 average on InterCode-4B, which is the closest thing to our sleep-frozen vs sleep-running cell, but slopes over the test stream are not reported, and the slow loop was run once on training data, not continued during deployment. Key differences from our setup: memory lives in an external retrieval store, not in the LoRA (the LoRA holds the four behaviours and some "internalized" execution); the update is on-policy KL distillation from a privileged self-teacher, not SFT on the child's own written frames; training is on 7k tasks from separate environments, not on the child's lived episodes; the teacher's hindsight requires many repeats of the same memory across a task group to estimate V(m), which our small-episode childhood lacks. What transfers directly: the four-way decomposition of what to teach, the "write root cause, not generic advice" target, discretionary write counts, and the idea of scoring a memory by whether episodes that carried it went better.
result.evidence_scale: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 and Qwen3.5-9B backbones (LoRA adapter released), trained on 7,000 tasks from AWM/Nemotron-Terminal-Corpus/EnvScaler and evaluated on disjoint LifelongAgentBench (DB/OS), MemoryArena (Math/Physics), AMA-Bench (CI/SU/SA), InterCode (Bash/CTF/SQL) and MiniHack; OPD-Evolver-9B beats the strongest same-backbone memory baseline on all 10 subsets (e.g. OS 65.0 vs 61.0, CTF 57.0 vs 53.0, SQL 64.01), beats Step-3.5-Flash-196B on 9/10 and Qwen3.5-397B-A17B on 6/10 subsets, and beats GRPO/Skill0/MemRL/Complementary-RL on 5/6 MiniHack+InterCode subsets. Controls: all memory methods start from an empty store and accumulate only from the evaluation stream with the same success/fail feedback; training-based baselines were trained on the same MiniHack data; ablations on InterCode-4B (avg 38.67) show w/o attribution 32.13, w/o slow loop 33.10, w/o selection/writing/maintenance smaller drops; single seed, no confidence intervals reported.

result.title: Learning to Learn-at-Test-Time: Language Agents with Learnable Adaptation Policies
result.authors: Zhanzhi Lou, Hui Chen, Yibo Li, Qian Wang, Bryan Hooi (National University of Singapore)
result.venue_or_status: arXiv preprint (v3, cs.LG); no venue marker found on the abs page. Code: github.com/zzzlou/meta-ttl (pushed 2026-04-01).
result.sections_read: Abstract; 1 Introduction; 2 Related Work; 3 Methodology (3.1 TTL formulation and W-AUC, 3.2 actor/meta-agent, 3.3 reflective meta-training, Algorithm 1); 4 Experiments (4.1 setup, 4.2 RQ1 main results Tables 1-5, 4.3 RQ2 Actor-GEPA / GRPO / parameter-based TTL Tables 6-9, 4.4 RQ3 fact-bank ablation Table 10); 5 Conclusion; Appendix A (expert selection, z-scores), B (skeleton headers only; bodies not in HTML), C (emergent properties of the optimized meta-prompt), D (26-iteration optimisation trajectory), E (case studies Detective, Temple, Balances). Also the GitHub README (evaluation flags: 3 seeds x 5 repeats, 6 episodes, 50-step limit).
result.what_is_learned_and_how: Nothing in weights changes at any stage of the main method. Two prompts change: (i) at test time, inside a K-episode "TTL session" on one task, a separate meta-agent LLM governed by a meta-prompt phi reads the trajectory history H_k after each episode and rewrites the frozen actor's system prompt rho_{k+1} ~ f_phi(. | rho_k, H_k) -- "updating rho is the sole mechanism for changing the actor's behavior across episodes"; the environment resets each episode so all improvement must come from that rewrite. (ii) At meta-training time, the meta-prompt phi itself is learned by gradient-free "reflective prompt evolution" (GEPA-style): sample a parent phi from an expert pool and a training task, run a TTL session, have a proposer LM reflect on the session and propose a revised phi, keep it only if it raises W-AUC on the same task (local gate), then re-score on all validation tasks and replace per-task experts where it is a new best; finally pick one phi* by highest average (z-scored) validation score. The signal is W-AUC = sum_k k*J(tau_k) / sum_k k*J_max, a learning-curve area with later episodes weighted more, i.e. the outer loop optimises the slope of test-time improvement, not the level. At deployment phi* is frozen and applied to unseen tasks; the seed phi_0 was the one sentence "analyze the game trajectory and provide feedback" (validation W-AUC 0.188), and 26 iterations (~27 h) took it to 0.407.
result.what_it_tells_us_to_parent: The paper's learned adaptation policy is, in effect, a written specification of how to reflect after an episode so that the reflection becomes usable conditioning for the next attempt -- exactly the disposition a parent would install. Its emergent components (Appendix C) are concrete teachables: (1) "Mandatory structured output" -- six required sections: diagnosis of what happened, durable game facts, next-episode priorities, a recommended route with save points, a concrete command script (first 15-25 moves), and parser tips, which "forces the meta-agent to separate diagnosis, fact extraction, planning, and scripting rather than producing a monolithic narrative"; (2) an "explicit credit assignment protocol" -- itemise which actions scored points and how to reproduce them, which caused death or threats, which wasted turns (dead ends, loops), which blocked progress; (3) "grounded fact accumulation" -- a "Game facts to remember" section recording map links, triggers, working syntax and rejected verbs, constrained to be "evidenced by the most recent episode log, preventing hallucination" (their version of our provenance gate); (4) "exploration management" -- at most one new experiment per episode, under a save/restore point, with a fallback if two attempts fail; (5) "concrete action scripts" that reproduce known scoring actions before trying new objectives; (6) a "CRITICAL ADAPTATION RULE": identify the actual situation from the log and ignore stored facts that do not apply (discovered at iteration 7 after the proposer had overfitted to Detective). The case studies show what the untaught behaviour looks like: the Naive meta-agent gives generic advice ("LOOK, then EXAMINE all notable objects") that does not use the episode's observations, and scores stagnate (89-131); the taught one names the specific blocker and the fix ("confronted the dazed man without the pistol ... GET PISTOL ... SHOOT DAZED MAN WITH PISTOL"), 114 -> 319 in one cycle. The fact-bank ablation shows the transferable part is the form of reflection, not the remembered content: removing facts raises OOD W-AUC (0.28 -> 0.34 GPT-5; 0.26 -> 0.31 GLM-5) while lowering ID. Meta-level lesson for the parent itself: judge a reflection habit by the learning curve it produces (W-AUC), and use semantically informed corrections ("the proposer diagnoses why the current candidate fails and generates a targeted fix") rather than random variation.
competencies_implied: structure post-episode reflection into diagnosis / facts / priorities / route / script
explicit credit assignment: what scored, what killed, what wasted turns, what blocked
extract durable facts only when evidenced by the log (provenance gate)
separate durable facts from episode-specific diagnosis
convert diagnosis into a concrete next-episode action script
exploit known route first, then one disciplined experiment per episode
fallback rule after repeated failure of the same approach
identify the situation before applying stored knowledge; ignore irrelevant facts
turn-budget awareness
separate task-agnostic strategy from domain knowledge
rewrite own instructions between episodes
evaluate a learning habit by its learning-curve slope (W-AUC)
targeted, diagnosed revision of the learning rule rather than random mutation
result.relevance_to_links: Link A (the write): Meta-TTL's write is a system-prompt rewrite by a second model, not a weight change; but the content of a good write is spelled out and empirically selected -- structured sections, itemised credit assignment, facts constrained to the most recent log, concrete scripts. Their evidence-grounding constraint (iteration 14: "only restate facts supported by the most recent log") is an independent discovery of our provenance rule, and their Naive-vs-Opt case studies are the same contrast as our synthetic-vs-child-authored gap: an unstructured reflection leaves no usable artifact. Table 9 is also a useful negative control for our regime: Online SFT on raw (state, action) pairs from the actor's own trajectories, Online GRPO and SFT+MAML on a Qwen3-8B actor gave weak and unstable gains (ID W-AUC 0.116/0.118/0.122 vs Static 0.084) -- consistent with "raw experience is not good post-training data"; they did not try training weights on articulated reflections, which is our gap. Link B (parenting installs the form): the outer loop is a parent -- a proposer LM reads a whole learning session and rewrites how the learner reflects, keeping changes only if the learner then learns faster; the installed thing is a form of thinking (six-section reflection, credit assignment, exploration discipline), and the fact-bank ablation shows the form, not the facts, is what transfers OOD. The seed prompt ("analyze the trajectory and provide feedback") is the unparented baseline. Difference: their form is installed by scored evolutionary selection over ~26 proposals with a scalar slope objective, not by dialogue, and it lives in a separate stronger model (GPT-5) rather than in the learner. Link C (integrated loop improves later learning): their objective is literally the slope (W-AUC weights episode k by k), and the headline result is that the same frozen actor improves faster across episodes on unseen tasks when the adaptation policy was learned (Jericho OOD W-AUC 0.23 -> 0.28, 0.34 without fact banks; tau2 OOD 0.33 -> 0.37) -- the closest published analogue of H2, in prompt space. In our 2x2 terms it is "parented, learning-policy frozen at deployment, episodic write running": phi* never changes after meta-training, so the paper has no test of continued consolidation of the how-to-learn itself, and the actor's prompt memory is reset per task session (no cross-task accumulation except the fact banks baked into phi*). Where it differs from a frozen base + one LoRA rewritten at sleep from the child's own thinking: (1) two models, the child does not author its own reflection; (2) memory is external, inspectable text, and the authors explicitly argue that separating strategies from facts "would not be possible if the policy were encoded in model weights" -- a claim H1 (retention and out-of-context expression in the LoRA) must answer; (3) no sleep: the write is applied immediately as context, so there is no repetition or consolidation step; (4) the meta-learning signal is a verifiable scalar reward per task, whereas our parent's feedback is verbal.
result.evidence_scale: Frozen Gemini-3-Flash actor in all main tables; meta-agent backbones GPT-5, GLM-5, Gemini-3-Flash (each independently meta-trained); Qwen3-4B meta-agent for the GRPO comparison; Qwen3-8B actor for the parameter-based TTL comparison. Tasks: Jericho (3 ID games Detective/Zork1/Temple, 3 OOD Balances/Library/Zork3; 6 episodes/session, 50 steps), WebArena-Lite (ID Shopping/GitLab/Map, OOD Reddit/Shopping Admin; 5 episodes), tau2-bench (ID Airline/Retail, OOD Telecom; 3 episodes); README indicates 3 seeds x 5 repeats. Headline: Jericho ID avg score 50.4 -> 110.8 (W-AUC 0.18 -> 0.41) vs Naive meta-agent, OOD 0.23 -> 0.28; WebArena-Lite ID W-AUC 0.57 -> 0.61 (GPT-5), 0.55 -> 0.64 (GLM-5); tau2 OOD 0.33 -> 0.37. Controls: Naive meta-agent (same architecture, unoptimised prompt), Reflexion, Memory Agent, TextGrad/EvoPrompt/EvoTest, Actor-GEPA with matched offline budget (Meta-TTL better on 10/11 tasks), GRPO outer loop (matched or beaten with 272 vs 1,920 rollouts), Online SFT/GRPO/SFT+MAML weight-update baselines, fact-bank ablation. No confidence intervals or significance tests appear in the sections read; WebArena OOD gains are within 0.01-0.03.

result.title: Training Language Agents to Learn from Experience
result.authors: Yuval Shalev, Zifeng Ding, Mateja Jamnik (University of Cambridge)
result.venue_or_status: arXiv preprint, cs.LG, v1 only; no venue or "comments" field on the abs page. Code released as MetaGym (github.com/yuvalshalev1/MetaGym).
result.sections_read: Full HTML (arxiv.org/html/2605.20477): abstract, 1 Introduction, 2 Related Work, 3 The In-context Training Task (Algorithm 1, Eqs. 1-3), 4 Training LLMs to Learn from Experience (dataset creation, reward Eq. 4, GRPO procedure), 5.1 Setup and environments, 5.2 Results (Tables 1-2, Figure 4 discussion), 5.3 Limitations, 6 Conclusion. PDF pages 12-16 via VM for Appendix A (reflector system prompt and user template, which the HTML stripped), B (compute/hyperparameters), C (MetaGym), D/E (actor prompts and trajectory examples).
result.what_is_learned_and_how: Weights change only in a separate "reflector" LLM (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, full RL fine-tune with GRPO via verl, lr 3e-6, 8 rollouts/group, KL 0.001); the "actor" LLM (also Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct) stays frozen and its policy is changed only through its system prompt. At test time, learning is purely in-context/prompt-level: in the "In-context Training (ICT)" loop the reflector reads the previous system prompt sp_{i-1} plus a batch of k=3 or 5 full actor trajectories (observations, actions, Success: Yes/No, total reward) on unseen tasks, each tried once, and emits ANALYSIS + IMPROVED PROMPT; the new prompt is scored on a fixed held-out validation set and the best is kept over N=10 meta-turns. At train time the signal is environment reward only, no human examples: a dataset of (sp_i, obs_i, task batch) tuples is collected by running the base model through 128 ICT loops x 4 turns; for each tuple the reflector samples G candidate prompts and each is rewarded by replaying the same previous batch with the frozen actor under the candidate (Eq. 4, "If I had the opportunity to try the same batch of tasks again, what would I do differently?"), while the reflector is explicitly prompted to write for future tasks to "discourage in-context overfitting" to that batch. Task types are split into meta-train and meta-test so the reflector cannot memorise a good prompt; it must extract the lesson in-context from the trajectories at inference.
result.what_it_tells_us_to_parent: The paper isolates one learning-process behaviour and shows it is trainable: reading a batch of one's own (actor) trajectories and distilling them into reusable, cross-task instructions rather than single-task self-correction. The externalised form is fixed by the reflector prompt: (1) "Identify what went well and what went wrong in the agent's behaviour", (2) "Diagnose how the current system prompt contributed to those outcomes", (3) "Write an improved system prompt that addresses the identified weaknesses ... for future episodes", output in two sections, ANALYSIS then IMPROVED PROMPT, the latter "written to be used directly without modification". It also prescribes a calibration disposition a parent could teach: when the prompt "succeeds on one task in the batch but fails on the others" the reflector "should analyse the factors that contributed to the successful case and generalise them to the remaining tasks"; when it "succeeds on all tasks" it "should generate a new system prompt that remains highly similar to the previous one, potentially reproducing it exactly" (do not churn what works). The lessons that emerge are generic task-family rules ("in maze-solving tasks, avoid revisiting the same path"; on unseen Cool-and-Place the reflector "observes that the actor is struggling to understand how to cool the objects" and writes "look for the fridge"; on unseen MiniHack-Read it "deduces that the goal ... is to find the item and read it"). Two measured findings matter for parenting: the untrained model already has this ability "to some extent" (the reflector-of-base already beats sp0), so the skill is latent and RL sharpens it, and the trained skill continues to compound past the training horizon (prompts keep improving beyond meta-turn 4 and 25% of best ALFWorld k=3 prompts appear only at turn 10). The paper's own word for the target: "learning from experience is itself a learnable meta-skill".
competencies_implied: extract reusable lesson from a batch of own trajectories
diagnose which instruction caused which outcome
generalise from the one success to the failures
leave a working rule unchanged (no churn on all-success)
write the lesson as directly usable instructions for future unseen tasks
articulate analysis before rewriting (ANALYSIS then IMPROVED PROMPT)
iterate own instructions across meta-turns beyond the training horizon
learn from single, non-repeatable attempts
result.relevance_to_links: Link A (the write): this is a write into a prompt, not into weights; the "memory" is a system prompt of at most ~2k tokens rewritten each meta-turn, and the frozen actor is the same base Qwen2.5-7B we use. It therefore shows the content side of A, that self-produced trajectory outcomes can be compressed into a compact, transferable, instruction-form artifact by a 7B model, but not the consolidation side; nothing is stored in the actor's weights and the artifact must be re-supplied in context. Link B (parenting installs the form): strong analogue. The form of the reflection (what went well/wrong, how the instruction caused it, rewrite for future tasks) is imposed by a fixed prompt, and RL with an environment-derived reward makes the reflector better at filling that form on unseen task types and even across benchmarks (MiniHack-trained k=5 reflector beats untrained Qwen on 4/6 ALFWorld types). That is "the disposition to produce good post-training data about experience is trainable", stated in their terms as a learnable meta-skill, with a frozen actor so the reflector's output is the only thing that changed. Their reward is replay of the same batch with an explicit instruction to write for future tasks, a mechanical analogue to our provenance gate (every rewritten instruction traces to an observed trajectory) and worth citing. Link C (integrated loop improves later learning): partially supported, in-context only. Figure 4 shows the slope continues past turn 4 and best prompts keep arriving late, i.e. the reflector's own outputs become better inputs for its next reflection; but the loop is in the prompt, there is no sleep and no weight update at deployment, and the reflector is a second model, not the child reflecting on itself (they list single-model actor-reflector and lifelong prompt updating as future work). Differences from our design: two models (frozen actor plus fully fine-tuned reflector) vs one frozen base with one LoRA; RL from environment reward vs SFT on the child's own thought output at sleep; memory as re-injected system prompt vs weight memory retrieved by completion; lessons aimed at task-family generalisation on a held-out set with a fixed validation stopping criterion vs discretionary, graded-importance memory over a whole life. It is a clean prior result for "the reflection skill is learnable and transfers across tasks" (H1-shaped, at the prompt level) and does not test H2 (does carrying the skill make later weight-level learning faster).
result.evidence_scale: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct for both actor and reflector; four reflectors trained (ALFWorld k=3/5, MiniHack k=3/5), ~20 GH200-hours each, 168 node-hours total. Held-out task types: ALFWorld Cool-and-Place 42.4 to 49.2% (k=3) and Pick Two 34.6 to 42.5% (k=3), 28.3 to 41.2% (k=5); MiniHack Dark/Read/PutOn/Zap gains of roughly 3-11 points, one loss (Zap k=3, 18.8 to 14.1%); 10 seeds x 10 meta-turns per cell, best prompt per run selected on a fixed validation set, standard deviations reported. Controls: initial prompt sp0, untrained Qwen reflector at the same k, type-level meta-train/meta-test split to rule out prompt memorisation, frozen actor to isolate prompt evolution; cross-benchmark transfer (MiniHack reflector on ALFWorld) 4/6 wins at k=5, but k=3 transfer is negative on several types.

result.title: Online Experiential Learning for Language Models
result.authors: Tianzhu Ye*, Li Dong*, Qingxiu Dong, Xun Wu, Shaohan Huang, Furu Wei (Microsoft Research; *equal contribution)
result.venue_or_status: arXiv preprint (cs.CL), Microsoft Research "Experiential Learning" series Part II (Part I = On-Policy Context Distillation, arXiv 2602.12275); code at aka.ms/oel-code. No peer-review venue listed.
result.sections_read: Full HTML text (arxiv.org/html/2603.16856v2): abstract, Sec 1 Intro, Sec 2 Preliminary, Sec 3.1-3.3 method + Algorithm 1, Sec 4.1-4.6 experiments and analysis (Tables 1-2), Sec 5 related work, Sec 6 conclusion, Appendix A (reverse-KL derivation), Appendix B (Self-Trajectory variant, Algorithm 2). PDF pages 11-18 via VM for Appendix C (game prompts Figs 8-9, extraction/solving prompt templates Figs 10-12, hyperparameter Tables 3-4) and Appendix D (Fig 13 example experience items). Figures 1, 4-7 are images; their content taken from captions and the surrounding text.
result.what_is_learned_and_how: Weights change (full-model update on Qwen3, lr 1e-6 to 5e-6; not LoRA), but via an intermediate text artifact. Stage 1 (extraction): the deployed policy itself (pi_extract = pi_theta) reads each multi-turn trajectory of actions and textual environment feedback and writes "transferable experiential knowledge" e_i, accumulated recursively across n=15-50 trajectories (e_i = [e_{i-1}; e_i'], conditioning on prior knowledge), repeated K=10 seeds to give a knowledge set C; the signal is purely textual game feedback (legal/wall/hole/goal + map), with no reward, labels or human annotation. Stage 2 (consolidation): "on-policy context distillation" -- the student pi_theta samples a single-turn response y from a partial rollout prefix x (no knowledge in context) and is trained to minimise token-level reverse KL against a frozen copy of itself conditioned on e (teacher = pi_theta(.|e, x)), so the knowledge-conditioned self acts as a dense token-level reward model and no environment access is needed at training time. The two stages iterate as an "online learning loop": redeploy, collect better trajectories, extract richer knowledge, consolidate again (2-3 rounds shown). All of this happens at "test time" in the deployment sense (learning from real interactions after release) but the parameter update is a server-side offline step between deployment rounds -- structurally a wake/sleep cycle.
result.what_it_tells_us_to_parent: The paper hardcodes, in a prompt, exactly the reflective behaviour a parent would want the child to own. The extraction prompt tells the model it "continuously refines its internal experience" and must "conduct a deep, comparative analysis to infer the game rules and the fundamental principles behind winning and losing", "hypothesize the game rules and effective winning strategies", and produce "1-2 concise, high-level, and widely applicable experience items" that are "generally useful rather than only applicable for the current map" -- i.e. abstract from the episode to a transferable rule, and label hypotheses as hypotheses (the solving prompt says the experience "is only a guess of how the game works, and the rules and strategies may be incomplete or incorrect"). It also installs incremental, non-redundant accumulation: "Do not repeat the previous experience. Make sure the newly generated experience is different", so each write must add to what is already known (conditioning on e_{i-1}). Example items (Fig 13) are the target register: rules ("the true objective is ... to reach the goal marked by 'O'"), strategies ("axis-aligned convergence" / reduce Manhattan distance), and named failure modes ("relying on hypothetical or future board states ... leads to invalid moves"; "validate every move against the current board state before submission"). Two measured facts a parent can use: (1) extracted knowledge beats raw trajectories both in context (18.2 vs 10.9%) and after consolidation (21.4 vs 7.8%; raw trajectories consolidated are no better than nothing, 7.5%) -- so the articulated lesson, not the replayed experience, is what is trainable; (2) knowledge the model wrote from its own trajectories beats knowledge written by a stronger model (31.1 vs 22.7% consolidated for Qwen3-1.7B) -- "on-policy consistency", i.e. the child's own words about its own experience are better training data than a smarter outsider's summary. Also: consolidated behaviour becomes shorter (response length to ~70% by round 3) -- internalised knowledge shows up as less deliberation, a measurable signature of a learned skill.
competencies_implied: extract transferable lesson from a trajectory
infer rules and win/lose principles from environment feedback
abstract beyond the current instance (generally useful, not map-specific)
hypothesise and flag uncertainty of own rules
accumulate without repeating prior knowledge
name failure modes and validation habits
write own experience in own words (on-policy consistency)
consolidate context into weights between deployment rounds
iterate: redeploy, re-extract, re-consolidate
result.relevance_to_links: Link A (the write): strong prior-regime evidence that the write should be a distilled, transferable, own-authored lesson rather than raw experience -- Table 1 is the cleanest published number showing raw-trajectory consolidation does nothing (7.8 vs 7.5% baseline) while extracted knowledge does (21.4%), and Table 2 shows the writer must be the learner itself (self-written 31.1 vs stronger-model-written 22.7%). This is the same claim as our synthetic-vs-child-authored gap (SEQ-049), measured at the consolidated-weights level, and cites Reflexion/ExpeL as the in-context/external-memory predecessors. Provenance is built in: every item traces to a trajectory plus environment feedback, matching our "model compresses, does not originate" defence. Link B (parenting installs the form): OEL does NOT test this -- the reflective form is a fixed prompt (Fig 10/11) applied by the system, never taught into weights; the model is not trained to extract without the prompt. It is the hardcoded baseline that our parenting aims to replace with a learned, discretionary disposition, so it is the natural control/ablation partner: "prompted extraction at sleep" vs "child that has internalised the extraction habit". Link C (integrated loop improves later learning): supportive -- Figures 4/7 show per-round gains persist across 2-3 rounds and across 1.7B/4B/8B ("each new iteration starts from a stronger baseline ... extract increasingly sophisticated experiential knowledge"), and consolidation surpasses the in-context ceiling, which is a slope claim of the H2 kind; but there is no 2x2 (no parented-vs-not arm, only frozen-vs-iterated on the same task) and no unseen-task transfer -- OOD is only IF-Eval preservation, not faster learning elsewhere. Differences from our setup: full-parameter update on Qwen3 (not frozen Qwen2.5-7B + one LoRA); training signal is reverse-KL to a knowledge-conditioned frozen self (context distillation), not SFT on the child's own written frames; knowledge is a growing text buffer truncated at 2048-8192 tokens, sampled randomly per prefix, rather than short canonical frames with repetition; the teacher is the model itself with the memory in context, so the "parent" is entirely absent -- environment feedback alone is the outside source. Their mechanism (student without context matches self with context) is a plausible alternative compile step for our memory adapter and deserves a note as a candidate for the "compile for memory" slot; their preservation-of-OOD result (on-policy beats off-policy forward-KL SFT on teacher samples) is a warning that plain SFT on generated text may forget more.
result.evidence_scale: Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B (thinking) and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (non-thinking), full-parameter training, on two TextArena games with rules stripped (Frozen Lake 3x3 with 2 holes; Sokoban 6x6 one box), up to 5 turns, 1024 tokens/turn; 20-100 distillation steps x 64 games per round, 2-3 OEL rounds; pass rate on 128 held-out maps averaged over 10 seeds. Headline: Sokoban Qwen3-4B-Instruct 7.5% -> 21.4% after one consolidation with extracted knowledge vs 7.8% with raw trajectories; Frozen Lake Qwen3-1.7B 7.3% -> 31.1% with self-extracted knowledge vs 22.7% with Qwen3-4B-extracted; response length drops to ~70% by round 3; IF-Eval strict accuracy preserved under on-policy distillation but degrades under off-policy context distillation. Controls: no-experience baseline, raw-trajectory vs extracted-knowledge (in-context and consolidated), self vs larger-model knowledge source, on- vs off-policy distillation; fixed steps and final checkpoint with no selection; no comparison to RL with rewards and no arm testing an unseen task's learning rate.

result.title: Self-Adapting Language Models (SEAL)
result.authors: Adam Zweiger*, Jyothish Pari*, Han Guo, Ekin Akyürek, Yoon Kim, Pulkit Agrawal (MIT CSAIL, Improbable AI Lab; * equal contribution)
result.venue_or_status: arXiv preprint (v2 Sep 2025). No venue stated on the arXiv page or the project page (jyopari.github.io/posts/seal); code released.
result.sections_read: Full HTML v2: abstract; 1 Introduction; 2 Related Work; 3 Methods (3.1 General Framework incl. Alg. 1 and ReST-EM derivation, 3.2 Domain Instantiations); 4 Results (4.1 few-shot ARC Table 1, 4.2 knowledge incorporation Table 2, Fig 4-5); 5 Limitations (catastrophic forgetting Fig 6, compute, context-dependent evaluation); 6 Discussion; Appendix A.1-A.4 (ARC setup, LoRA configs, compute); Appendix B.1-B.11 (SQuAD setup, ReST-EM procedure, LoRA r=64/alpha 128 for policy SFT, hyperparameter search spaces, grading, SEM table, 3B vs 7B scaling, Generative Adapter and Entigraph comparisons, proxy reward, seven prompt variants Table 10).
result.what_is_learned_and_how: Two nested weight changes. Inner loop (test-time and train-time): given a new context C (a SQuAD passage, or ARC few-shot demos), the model generates a "self-edit" SE in natural language -- for knowledge incorporation a list of "implications derived from the content" (restatements, inferences, atomic facts); for ARC a tool specification choosing data augmentations (rotations, flips, size, chain, repeat) and optimisation hyperparameters (learning rate, epochs, loss over all tokens vs output tokens only) -- and the model is then SFT'd on that self-edit (LoRA r=32-64 for single passage, full finetuning for continued pretraining over 200/2067 passages), giving theta'. Outer loop (train-time only): RL over the self-edit generation policy using as reward whether theta' answers held-out questions about the passage (or the ARC test grid) correctly; GRPO/PPO were unstable so they use ReST-EM = rejection sampling + SFT: 50 contexts x 5 self-edits x 3 seeds, keep the single best self-edit per context, SFT the policy on the 50 winning (prompt -> self-edit) pairs with LoRA r=64, two rounds (~6h on 2xH100 per round, each self-edit evaluation 30-45 s). The learned policy converges within two rounds to "an edit style that distills the passage into easily learnable atomic facts", i.e. longer and more detailed self-edits (Fig 5). The RL state formally includes theta, so training must be on-policy; nothing is stored outside the weights (no external memory store). At deployment the trained model writes one self-edit per new passage and is finetuned on it, no reward needed.
result.what_it_tells_us_to_parent: SEAL's learned behaviour is precisely "produce good post-training data about a new input", and it isolates which parts of that behaviour matter. (1) Raw experience is not good training data: finetuning on the passage itself gives 33.5% vs 32.7% base ("using the raw data alone is insufficient"); the child must "restructure the information" -- the paper's student analogy is "assimilating and rewriting the information in the form of notes". (2) The form of the write is the dominant lever and is externally installed: with no RL at all, prompt format alone moves single-passage accuracy from 39.7 (implications) to 49.3 (implications-long) and 49.4 (rewrite the passage in different ways); the no-prompt condition, "letting the model determine its own self-edit format", collapses to 13.8 and only 18.9 after RL -- the base model does not have the disposition, someone must give it the form. (3) Write more and in more detail: RL "dramatically increased the length of the response"; the proxy-reward rubric that nearly matches full RL (45.6 vs 47.0, 5 min vs 6 h) grades self-edits on "length, diversity, quality, and correctness" -- a parent could grade a child's memory writes on exactly these four axes. (4) Judge writes by whether they later make you answer correctly without the source in context (the reward), and reinforce only the writes that did (ReST-EM = SFT on good self-edits) -- a sleep-time filter. (5) Decide how much to train on an experience: on ARC the model chooses learning rate, epochs and whether to compute loss on all tokens or only output tokens, and selecting these well lifts success from 20% to 72.5%. (6) Proposed but not done: the model should also "generate its own evaluation questions" while the content is still in context, so it can supervise its own learning without paired QA.
competencies_implied: restate a new input as implications and atomic facts
rewrite the same content in several forms
write long and detailed rather than terse
choose the write format (implications / rewrite / self-QA)
decide how much to train on an experience (LR, epochs, loss mask)
judge a write by later recall without the source in context
reinforce only the writes that improved performance
write own evaluation questions for new content (proposed)
result.relevance_to_links: Link A (the write): the strongest published evidence, on our exact base model (Qwen2.5-7B base, LoRA), that the content of what is written into weights at update time decides whether the fact is retrievable later: passage-only 33.5, self-written implications 39.7, self-written rewrites 55.6, GPT-4.1 implications 46.3, RL-trained self-edits 47.0 (Table 2, Table 10). It also confirms the Physics-of-LLMs/TMEM regime we adopt (many restatements, atomic facts, no-context recall as the test) and cites Allen-Zhu & Li directly. Link B (parenting installs the form): SEAL shows the disposition is absent in the base model (no-prompt 13.8-18.9) and is installed from outside -- by a prompt (worth ~10-16 points) and then sharpened by RL against a verifiable reward (worth a further 6-11 points in every format). In our terms the prompt is the parent's frame and the ReST-EM step ("SFT on good self-edits") is the sleep that consolidates good thought. Difference: SEAL's teacher signal is a downstream QA reward computed by actually finetuning and testing, not a parent's correction of the thought itself; and the form is prompted per passage at inference, whereas we want the form expressed unprompted from the LoRA (H1). Link C (integrated loop improves later learning): SEAL is a meta-learning result on isolated episodes -- it shows the write-policy generalises (from single passages to CPT over 200 passages, 58.2) and that the gain over base self-edits grows with capacity (1.75x at 3B vs 2.04x at 7B), but it does not test whether a model carrying the skill learns faster over a sequence; its sequential experiment (Fig 6, 8 passages) shows monotone forgetting with no retention mechanism, and the adapted theta' is discarded per passage in the main setting. So SEAL supports the premise of H2 (the data-generation disposition is a trainable skill that transfers) but leaves the slope claim open. Differences from our frozen base + one LoRA rewritten at sleep: SEAL updates the policy itself (LoRA r=64 SFT on winning self-edits) and separately trains a fresh inner LoRA per passage, i.e. two loops and no single accumulating adapter; the self-edit is elicited by a fixed prompt, not free first-person thought during acting; content is grounded in the in-context passage (provenance is trivially satisfied) but "implications" may include inferences, which our provenance gate would need to source; reward is an external verifiable task, so SEAL cannot train on unlabeled experience (their stated limitation), which is exactly the gap the parent fills for us. Also note their finding that chain-of-thought before writing did not help (38.7 vs 39.7) -- reflection without articulated artefacts adds nothing, matching our diagnosis.
result.evidence_scale: Knowledge incorporation: Qwen2.5-7B base (and 3B), SQuAD v1.1 no-passage QA, 200 eval passages / 974 questions, GPT-4.1 grader; single-passage LoRA: base 32.7, passage-only 33.5, base self-edits 39.7, GPT-4.1 synthetic 46.3, SEAL 47.0; CPT full-FT n=200: 58.2 (GPT-4.1 59.4, Entigraph 56.0), n=2067: 46.4 (GPT-4.1 49.2, Entigraph 48.6); two ReST-EM rounds of 50 contexts x 5 edits x 3 seeds. Few-shot: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct on 11 train / 8 eval curated ARC tasks, success 72.5% vs 20% (self-edit w/o RL), 0% ICL, 100% oracle TTT. Controls: passage-only, un-RL'd self-edits, GPT-4.1 data, Entigraph, Generative Adapter, 7 prompt variants with and without RL, proxy rubric reward, 3B vs 7B, 8-step continual-edit forgetting curve with SEMs ~0.03.

result.title: Scaling Self-Evolving Agents via Parametric Memory
result.authors: Tao Ren, Weiyao Luo, Hui Yang, Rongzhi Zhu, Xiang Huang, Yuchuan Wu, Bingxue Chou, Jieping Ye, Jiafeng Liang, Yongbin Li, Yijie Peng (Qwen-Character Team, Alibaba Group; Peking University)
result.venue_or_status: arXiv preprint, v1 only; no venue stated in the paper
result.sections_read: Identity via arXiv API (search all:TMEM AND all:memory returned exactly one matching paper) plus arxiv.org/html/2606.04536 and the PDF pages 3-4 via the VM. Read in full: abstract; Sec. 1 Introduction; Sec. 2 Related Work; Sec. 3 (agentic decision process, Eq. 1-7, Fig. 1 memory-writing prompt text recovered from the PDF, 3.1 fast-weight rollout dynamics, 3.2 SVD initialisation, Theorem 1); Sec. 4 stop-gradient policy optimisation (Eq. 8-9); Sec. 5.1 setup and implementation details, 5.2 pre-RL results (Tables 1-3), 5.3 post-RL results (Figs. 3-4 text), 5.4 ablations (Tables 4-6, Fig. 5 text), 5.5 efficiency (Table 7); Sec. 6 Discussion; Sec. 7 Conclusion; Appendix A (theorem proof), Appendix C (Table 8 unfiltered CL-Bench), Appendix D/E figure captions. Not read: Appendix B derivation; case-study figures are images. Note the lead's phrase 'self-written canonical pairs' is not the paper's term; the paper says 'grounded SFT QA pairs'.
result.what_is_learned_and_how: Two things change at two timescales. (1) At test time, within a single episode: a small LoRA 'fast weight' Delta_t (rank 6, on gate/up/down FFN projections of the last 4 layers only; projection matrix A initialised from the top-r SVD of the pretrained weight and frozen, only B trained) is updated by a 'lightweight online SFT' (SGD, lr 5e-4, 5 epochs, batch 16) whenever working context + explicit memory exceeds a budget L_max (4096-12288 tokens). The training data for that update is the agent's own output under a memory-writing prompt d: a JSON array of {instruction, output} 'grounded SFT QA pairs' distilled from the session; the working context is then cleared and no textual memory is carried forward, so the facts survive only in Delta_t (Eq. 6). Updates are cumulative across triggers within the episode; the paper frames everything as 'intra-episode parametric self-evolution', so Delta_t is per-episode memory, not lifetime memory. (2) At training time, across episodes: the full base theta_0 is trained with GRPO (200 steps, batch 64, n=8, outcome reward only) with stop-gradient through the online update operator T, so the same reward trains both ordinary task/tool actions and the 'extraction actions' (Eq. 9); the base learns 'to produce supervision that makes its own future fast-weight updates useful'. Signal: for the write, self-generated QA pairs grounded in the session; for the writer, final task reward (F1/EM or rubric).
result.what_it_tells_us_to_parent: The paper's central move is to treat memory extraction as a policy behaviour rather than a fixed preprocessing step: 'memory extraction is not an auxiliary preprocessing step; it is an action whose quality determines the data used for later online adaptation', and RL on outcome reward makes the base 'not only capable at inference time but also easy to specialize through a small number of online LoRA updates'. The memory-writing prompt d (Fig. 1) is, in effect, a hard-coded parenting script for that behaviour, and its clauses map onto teachable moves: (a) discretionary quantity, 'Generate QA pairs adaptively based on how much useful information is present in the session ... If there is no usable evidence, return an empty JSON array'; (b) provenance, 'Each question must be answerable using explicit information from the session. Each answer must be concise, factual, and directly supported by the session'; (c) content beyond facts, 'capture the lessons learned from the session to help improve future interactions, such as preferences, plans, events, and temporal details, rather than just factual questions' (Appendix E Fig. 13 shows a separate 4-item 'long-dialogue handling experience' array, i.e. meta-lessons); (d) breadth of perception, 'Cover diverse types when possible: who/what/when/where, preferences, plans, events, and temporal details'; (e) 'Avoid duplicate or near-duplicate QA pairs'. Two measured results tell a parent which forms are worth teaching: the supervision-form ablation (Table 5, Qwen3-4B) shows the written artifact's form governs what the weights can hold, raw next-token on the transcript 10.37 F1 vs free-form summary 35.44 vs QA pairs 41.24 on LongMemEval-S ('trains the model to reproduce the raw context verbatim rather than distill task-relevant knowledge'), which is direct evidence that raw experience is poor post-training data and that query-aligned, self-contained frames are good; and the L_max bell curve (Fig. 5) shows when to write matters, too often 'discard[s] fine-grained details before they are absorbed', too rarely makes 'the extraction prompt harder to ground'. Finally, the writer is improvable by outcome: after RL, TMEM gains +5.12 F1 / +5.02 EM on LoCoMo versus +2.62/+2.46 (MemAgent) and +2.79/+3.54 (A-MEM), which the authors read as 'RL benefits are larger when the memory mechanism can adapt fast weights during the episode'.
competencies_implied: decide how much to write from information density (discretionary memory)
write nothing when there is no sourced evidence
ground every memory in explicit session evidence (provenance)
convert experience into query-aligned question-answer frames
extract lessons, preferences, plans and temporal detail, not only facts
perceive one episode from many angles (who/what/when/where)
avoid duplicate memories
write at a context-budget boundary rather than continuously
improve one's own extraction behaviour from downstream outcome
result.relevance_to_links: Link A (the write): strongest support. Self-authored QA pairs SFT'd into a rank-6 LoRA are retrievable at the end of the episode and beat prompt-space summary and retrieval memory on Qwen3-4B/8B (LongMemEval-S 41.87 vs 31.66 F1 at 8B, +10.21 F1 / +7.02 EM over the best explicit-memory baseline). Table 5 is the cleanest existing evidence that the form of the artifact, not the transcript, is what the write can store (QA 41.24 vs summary 35.44 vs raw 10.37 F1), and Table 4 shows few-step writes are sensitive to adapter initialisation (SVD vs random, +3.2 EM). This is the regime the project adopts and should cite rather than claim. Link B (parenting installs the form): TMEM installs the form by a fixed prompt plus GRPO on task reward, not by a parent, and the disposition lands in the full base theta_0, not in an adapter. It does show the form is a learnable policy (extraction tokens get gradient, and the writer's RL gain is roughly double the baselines'), and the Fig. 1 prompt is a ready-made 'numbered baseline' of the kind Rohin described (hard-coded rule, gym adds nuance). What it does not show is H1: that a taught extraction disposition survives in a LoRA and is expressed outside the context where it was taught; TMEM's disposition is always elicited by the same prompt d. Link C (integrated loop improves later learning): the post-RL comparison is the nearest analogue to an interaction effect, better writer x weight-write yields more gain than better writer x prompt memory, but it is a level after 200 RL steps on in-distribution benchmarks, not a slope on an unseen verifiable task, and there is no consolidation-frozen arm, so it is not a 2x2 and does not test H2. Numbers to treat cautiously: LoCoMo 4B F1 gap is 0.06, the 8B 4-objective search gain is called 'directional', CL-Bench was filtered by Qwen3-30A3B, and unfiltered CL-Bench totals are 4-5% for every method.
